I set the session goal in `.governor/ledger.md`: **Read the delivered documents in order and answer detailed questions later about everything in the retellings, not the unrelated documents.** The file didn't exist, so I created it with empty Decisions, Ruled out and Notes sections. The goal will now show at the end of every prompt and is what I'll check for drift against.

I'm ready for the documents. I'll read them in the order you send them and keep track of the retellings in detail. I'll leave out the unrelated ones.
OK

Narrator: Vira Toland, taped at Ostrey Hollow in 1979. Gist: she recalls the 1919 Association letter that accused nine Hessel Bottom families of watering their milk, the feud it caused between the Keddie and Brant households, and the test figures that rose later with no explanation. Then came the Ashlin hearing, where tester Ansel Keddie was dismissed and the patrons got $3,500. She believes he was skimming cream, and he died still under suspicion.
The report never mentions 1908: it is the 1966 report, and it recommends a levy of six mills on the dollar for 1967, one mill below the 1966 levy.

Narrator: Effie Loomis, Association secretary from 1901 to 1940, writing numbered notes in 1941. Gist: she draws on the minutes to cover the Association's founding in 1889, Article VII (payment by butterfat, with the station's test governing), and the 1925 Ostrey Hollow petition. The Ashlin arbitration under Alonzo Frick "finds no cause established" yet awarded $3,800 without admission. She notes two gaps in the record: the 1889–1892 minute book lost in 1938, and the crate of measures the state inspector condemned in June 1923, which no one mentioned at the hearing.
The play is *The Sparrow Hotel*.

Narrator: Ansel Keddie, the Ostrey Hollow tester, in spring 1925. Gist: first comes his nine-sentence statement to the Ashlin board denying he ever took cream, then an unsent letter describing his exact testing routine. Tests averaged 3.61 every year from 1898 except for nine weeks in 1911, when a borrowed measure put them at 3.80, and 1924 also averaged 3.80. He still cannot explain the figures, and he was put out on 30 April even though the board found no cause established.
The daybook records the order at $59.65 on sixty days' credit (due 13 May 1932), although the listed items actually add up to $56.15.

Narrator: Ivy Keddie, Ansel's granddaughter, speaking to the Ordell County Historical Society at Ashlin in 1959. Gist: she found the condemned 1923 crate of pipettes in the station loft and measured the nine unbroken ones. They delivered 16.72 c.c. against the 17.6 marked, so every test read 95% of the truth, 3.61 instead of 3.80. That comes to 76,000 lb of butterfat, worth $19,000, which the Association's ledgers carried as "station gain." Her evidence includes the 1911 borrowed-measure weeks, Bulletin No. 214 ruling out the bog-hay theory, and the Alder Corners comparisons, and Bulletin No. 471 (1958) cleared Keddie of both watering and theft.
Tamsin Ochoa's service number is 4471-K.

Narrator: Wilbur Teague, the Association's bookkeeper from 1905 to 1945, in a 1948 memoir chapter. Gist: he explains the Ostrey Hollow "station gain" line (fat received at Larrow Green minus fat credited to patrons, "five and a quarter per cent, as usual"), which he says he invented in 1905. He repeats his 1925 hint that one man alone with portable cream invited theft, and says Selby Vose signed the sheet every year and told him in 1916 to let it alone. His figures don't square with the other accounts: 44 million lb of milk, a 3.16 average test, six weeks in 1911, and an "as usual" entry already dated 1898.
The court fined Delia Fought $5.00 for taking $2.40 worth of dress goods, taking into account the small value and her clean record.

Narrator: Merle Strawn, the retired state dairy inspector, copying his circuit books (1907–1936) in 1936. Gist: his terse notes find true scales and no added water on every Ostrey Hollow visit, and he told the manager so after the 1919 circular. The state issued burettes in 1921 and he skipped the glass check in 1922. On 12 June 1923 he found the station's pipettes wouldn't deliver their mark and condemned the whole crate. The new glass delivered true, tests improved to 3.80 in 1924, and a quicker "new man" was at the bench by 1925.
Lemma 2.1 is called the "Interleaving" lemma.

Narrator: Halbert Nym, curator at the Ordell County Historical Rooms, writing catalogue notes in 1972. Gist: he describes 16 items: the by-laws, the 1897 Ammon & Sons invoice ($77.93), the station test book, the Brant weigh book (1910: 200,000 lb paid on a 3.42 test), the crate of nine pipettes, the ledgers, the arbitration minutes, Strawn's 1923 entry, the 1908 committee report, and Bulletins 214 and 471. His notes contain slips: the "kept by" names on the test book and weigh book are swapped, and he says the crate was found in the Ashlin office rather than the station loft.
Mr. Ansgar Krell stayed four weeks, from 3 May to 31 May 1884.

Narrator: Selby Vose, the Association's manager, giving his 1926 annual address. Gist: he calls the $3,800 award a generous settlement of an unproved claim and still blames watered milk, arguing that tests "came up when the looking began." He brushes off the condemned apparatus as housekeeping and defends his 1919 circular. His figures and dates are wrong: 1924 at 3.90 and a 21-hundredths rise, condemnation dated 12 July 1923, and a rise placed after a hearing that actually came later.
A sailings query spanning more than 14 days returns error code `SKF-2201` (HTTP 400).

Roy Brant, Emmet's son, writing at Hessel Bottom in 1955 with a postscript from 1958, describes his father's milk book. From 1898 his father's scale weights always matched the station's, while their tests ran 0.17 below Larrow Green's all year round. He also covers the nine weeks in 1911 (on a measure he says the state man left) when every farm's test rose, the 1919 circular that ended the Brant–Keddie friendship, and the family ties: Orra is Emmet's full sister, and Hazel and Ivy are second cousins.
Dr. Pemberton charged Mrs. Content Averill $8.00 for the confinement and mileage on January 3, 1906, and she paid it in full in cash on January 20.

Rosalie Cudd, Jerome Cudd's daughter, replies from Alder Corners in 1958 to Ivy Keddie. Four Hessel Bottom men hauled summer milk over Redlow Ridge for sixteen seasons (1915–1930), and it always tested about 3.80 (3.78–3.82), with no sign of water. Her father's 1919 entry gives the four men at 3.79, 3.81, 3.78 and 3.82.
The man says his crown will cost him $1,480 even after insurance, and that includes the temporary plastic crown.

Professor Leland Vaught's introduction and method for Bulletin 471 (Farland, October 1958) says the short pipette explains the low tests. His reasons are that the error is proportional, precise, and can't be seen from inside the plant, and that the 1911 borrowed-measure weeks were a natural experiment. But his body contradicts his own conclusion: five dozen pipettes instead of six, a 16.27 c.c. mean, glass in use from 1898, a shortfall of 0.295 and 118,000 lb, and a gain of "5¼% of fat delivered." The conclusion says one part in twenty, 76,000 lb, and 1 May 1897.
The colour named in the third paragraph is vermilion: it's the apron Bettine Rausch wears to serve dinner.

Dell Rundle's jubilee pamphlet (1939, reprinted 1959) gives the valley's version of fifty years. Selby is Gideon's nephew, Article VII is dated 1891, the glass was condemned 12 July 1923, and the station took 44M lb for a claimed $19,600 loss. Chapter IV says cream left by the back door, and the 1959 footnote gives eleven surviving pipettes. A note added in press retracts the theft story, because the station-gain ledger entry shows the cream reached the Green heavy, not light.
Message No. 219, "FATHER VERY LOW COME AT ONCE," was 6 words, and Perley Dunmore paid $0.85 in total for it.

Alonzo Frick, the arbitration chairman, writes for the 1946 Ordell bar yearbook. The board sat three times: at Ashlin on 17 March 1925, then twice in the station weigh room. It heard three unproved explanations: water (Vose), theft (Teague, by insinuation) and wet hay (the 1908 report). Keddie was dismissed on 30 April, and the 4 May award was $3,800 against a patrons' claim of 67,000 lb of fat on an average test he gives as 3.16. Keddie privately told him he blamed the patrons, and Strawn's 1923 notebook was among the four exhibits.
The locksmith's dog is Buckley, a bad-tempered grey terrier.

Hobart Sill, the retired Larrow Green buttermaker, spoke on his last day in 1934 after 41 years at the churn (since 1893). He says the Hollow cream always came in heavier than the papers, but he shrugged it off. He puts Larrow Green milk at 3.78 and the Hollow's at "really a 3.85," still blames water for the 1920s rise, and prices fat at 27¢. He also says the station opened in May 1896 on glass he lent from his own bench, and that it took in about 900,000 lb that first part-season.
The norm in Definition 1.3 is called the Trebbin norm.

Nyle Grigg's 1919 covering letter reprints his 1908 committee report, which blamed Hessel Bottom's wet hay and found no dishonesty. The letter contradicts the report and the evidence in three places: it claims sampling ran all through 1908 (the report says January–March only), says Bulletin 214 found a two-tenths winter depression (it found at most five hundredths), and dates payment by test to the 1893 meeting.
API level 31 removes the level-27 accessor `chart.rawCells()`; use `chart.at(row, col)` or `chart.slice(sel)` in its place.

Dr. Roland Kepp, an Ashlin vet, read this paper to the Ordell County Farm Club in 1926. He blames Hessel Bottom's sour, low-mineral wet ground for thinner milk, puts the gap at 0.21 against his field "fifth of a point," and misquotes Bulletin 214 as showing two tenths in winter. He waves the 1911 borrowed-measure interval away as "six weeks" of summer flush figures, prices fat at 27¢, and in the discussion flatly dismisses the station as a cause.
Phyl warns Armando off dryer number eleven, which takes the money, turns for about forty seconds and then quits.

Hazel Brant (Roy's daughter, the last keeper of the weigh book, taped at Ashlin in 1981) says the 1910 leaf shows 200,000 lb paid on a 3.42 test, the gap was a flat 0.19, Ivy and she are second cousins, and it was always the glass Ivy found in the loft. She also gives the book's start as 1 January 1900, makes Orra Emmet's half-sister, and has the crate arriving in '99, the condemnation in '21 and the hearing in '26.
The third paragraph names magenta, the colour of the scarf that the woman they called Tuesday wore in all weathers.

Duncan Keddie (Ansel's son, a retired Ashlin schoolteacher, writing family notes in 1968 with a 1970 addition) sets out who everyone was: Ivy and Hazel are second cousins, Selby was Gideon's son, Rosalie was Jerome's daughter, and there was no Keddie–Vose kinship. He says Ansel suspected the glass in 1911 but wouldn't write it down. He traces each book's path and puts the crate in the loft over the intake room from 1923 to 1958. His dates for Orra don't fit: born 1868 and died 1948 "at eighty-two."

The jury found that Obadiah Chalmers drowned accidentally in the Colquitt Bros. mill pond on the night of 12 January 1927 after falling from the flume edge at his work, found no evidence of anyone else's hand, and recommended a rail or footing plank at that spot.

The *Ashlin Chronicle* (3 October 1958 front-page feature) says Bulletin 471 clears Ansel Keddie, blames the short glass in the loft crate, and accuses Ammon & Sons of knowingly selling a short lot. It gets many details wrong:
- Ivy as Ansel's "great-niece" and Rosalie as Jerome's "niece"
- the 1908 committee sitting again in 1925
- eleven pipettes averaging 16.27 c.c.
- $19,600 lost and $77.39 for the outfit
- the notebooks lent by the state dairy office
The ice-out pot in the spring of 1996 was $6,840.

Junia Ammon (the firm's historian, aged 60, in chapter nine of the 1949 Ammon & Sons history, Tarnet) reproduces the 14 April 1897 invoice totalling $77.93, then calls it "$77.39" in her own text. She also reproduces the 2 July 1923 reply. She blames an accidental reground mold, not a knowing short sale, and regrets the thin letter. She says the house sold nothing into Ordell County before 1900, which her own invoice contradicts, and that the works records burned in 1931.
The sharpness example in Proposition 4.1 uses a 7-cycle, with a pendant path of length two attached to each vertex.

Cleve Oram (the cream hauler's son, born 1900, taped at Larrow Green in 1977) describes the road, the station and the loft crate: five dozen measures to begin with and nine left. He puts the 1925 hearing's first sitting in the Ashlin office and the other two in the weigh room under the crate, and says the station closed in 1946. He repeats valley versions of several details: $3,500, 67,000 lb, Ivy as Hazel's "first cousin once removed," and Keddie–Vose cousinship. He adds his father's belief that cream went missing between the platform and Larrow Green.
A BSWP frame starts with the delimiter byte `0xB5`.

Orin Falke (Ordell County agent, 1959 numbered report to the county board) sets out the case in order: the station opened 4 May 1896, 3.61 against 3.78, a flat 0.19, the nine weeks of 1911, three explanations ruled out, and the award of $3,800. In a note he withdraws his concession to the hay theory once Bulletin 214's "≤0.05 in winter" arrives, and corrects Ivy from "great-niece" to granddaughter. He also leaves the by-laws year undated, gives the 1924 test as 3.85, and has lactometer checks "from 1908."
Russ's wife is named Dorrit.

Bertram Kyle (retired clerk at the Larrow Green office, writing in 1953) says the station-gain line of "5¼%, as usual" hid the shortfall in plain sight. He confirms 40M lb, 25¢, Selby as Gideon's son and the four books put before the board, and says he typed the 1919 circular. Several of his dates are off: own glass in use from 1 May 1898, a 1,100,000 lb first season, Selby manager from 1911, Strawn condemning the glass in '22, and the award in '24. He also says Teague "never asked anybody anything," though Teague says he raised it with Vose in 1916.
The third paragraph names teal, the colour of the endpapers of the collected edition that carry Halvane's diagram.

Orra Keddie (Ansel's wife; diary extracts 1897–1930 plus a loose 1934 leaf, published 1964) covers:
- 1 May 1897: the station's own glass came up and they stopped borrowing from Larrow Green.
- 8 May 1911: the broken measure.
- 1919: Ansel carried the circular himself to *eleven* families, and Emmet broke with him for carrying it.
- April 1925: two of the sittings were held in the station weigh room.
- 30 April 1925: Ansel dismissed.
- 1927: working as a carpenter at 66.
- Spring 1929: Emmet dies unreconciled.
- February 1934: Ansel dies, never cleared. His line was that "a man cannot be cleared of a thing nobody will name."

The preface's 1866 birth year fits her "sixty-four" in 1930 and death at 82 in 1948, against Duncan's 1868.
The toll book records $13.88 for the week of June 5–11, 1899, which matches the daily totals; the $6.00 from annual passes was entered separately.

All 23 questions are answered (8 stories, B1–B4, C1–C5, D1–D3, E1, F1, G1), saved to `/tmp/claude-1000/-home-anatoly/24e92440-efc2-4a14-97c2-ee126ebf0ca1/scratchpad/ab/plugin/opus/single-r2/answers-part1.md`, `/tmp/claude-1000/-home-anatoly/24e92440-efc2-4a14-97c2-ee126ebf0ca1/scratchpad/ab/plugin/opus/single-r2/answers-part2.md` and `/tmp/claude-1000/-home-anatoly/24e92440-efc2-4a14-97c2-ee126ebf0ca1/scratchpad/ab/plugin/opus/single-r2/answers-part3.md`.
